translations.text: Of our holy father John Chrysostom.
A sermon for Holy Friday. Our labor of fasting has now come to an end.
And it ends with the cross. For where should a victorious struggle end,
if not at the monument of victory? For the cross is victorious.
It was planted once, but it drives out demons forever.
For where are the pagan temples and the wasteful slaughter of animals? Where are the shrines and the impious fire? Everything was extinguished by one thing: the holy blood fell.
And the cross stood firm: a mighty power, an invisible arrow, an immaterial medicine, a spring that relieves suffering, a glory subjected to scorn.

Even if I speak of other unheard-of things about Christ, even if I astonish the listener by proclaiming unheard-of miracles, I glory not so much in those things as in the cross. For example, I will say this:

Jesus came forth from a virgin. It is a great miracle to bypass marriage and break through the order of nature. But if there had been no cross, the first virgin of Paradise would not have been saved by her deeds.
But now, at the time of the cross, the first woman is saved, healing the ancient evil through new gifts of grace.
A dead man rose in Galilee, but he died again. But I, having risen because of the cross, can no longer fall into death.

Jesus, who is God, sailed the sea in a boat. Wood will give help on that day. But I have received the wood as an eternal blessing. Taking it in place of a ship, I drive back the spiritual waves of the crafty ones. Five thousand were fed, not by a single sign of the cross. Where, then, are the leftovers of that food? How shall I, who was not there, receive the leftovers of those who were there? For twelve baskets of fragments remained.

For that gift of grace was limited in number. Christ was crucified, and we are continually fed. Even when we have eaten our fill, we ask again; having received, we love, and our need becomes greater. For grace is never depleted. Let this day be praised, the world's parent, because of which the other days were appointed for rejoicing. How? Listen. Today Adam was created, on the sixth day. Today he bore the divine image. Today a little world was formed within the world. Today the human helmsman, the good oars of the inhabited world,

a living creature ruling over all living creatures. Today he received commandments for the exercise of his free will. Today he fell out of Paradise. Today he was admitted again. O day of many forms! O day of many tears and of no tears! O day that brought sorrow in the morning but joy in the evening! Indeed, it did not do as much harm as it brought healing. I confess to you that I am sorrowful as I pursue the sufferings of old, hearing of Adam cast out of his Father's house: a man who was a citizen of Paradise, living without working the earth, fed without rain, needing no sweat or spade or toil or running about to sustain his life, delighting in evergreen trees, passing from flower to flower,
passing from fruit to fruit. Following
a thought, having need to follow it, but, because of the beauty of the things he saw, having no [?] toward which to stretch out his hands first. Many times I wept over such great blessings,
seeing him deprived of them.
For the suffering was shared and touched our race as well. But when I looked into the Gospels and came to this day—for that day was the sixth, and so is this one.
But I have destroyed [?] and have left sorrow behind. I am radiant in my words, and I say to myself and to you: pain, sorrow, and sighing have fled away; the old things have passed away.
See, everything has become new. For just as physicians’ assistants heal snakebites,
taking healing herbs from them and mixing them with wines [?] to heal the injury, so the Savior also turned every evil cause to good, making human bitterness sweet,
turning it into healing, turning death’s sting back upon death itself, turning the injury caused by the tree into salvation, and taking away the day that had saddened the world.
and gave back a day that gladdened the world. Do not believe me, but your own eyes.
Look at this gathering, and stop [?] us with the day of the cross.
And let us all rejoice and fast from evil, and let us cleanse everything within and without. Such is the message of the feast; such is the form of its rejoicing.
I will tell a few of the wonders of the cross’s power. Look at the circle of the inhabited world:
how many villages and how many cities, how many places, how many nations, how many islands, how many rivers, how many coasts,

how many peoples, countries, and foreigners there are! They all fast because of the cross, having crucified their enemies through its power. For many, the night comes to an end, but the labor of fasting does not come to an end.
And now, why have we all gathered to hear something about the cross? We fill the churches, and [?] one another,
sweating and toiling, often being granted an audience before judges, but standing gladly before Jesus,
because Jesus stood for our sake, to halt the course of evil.
What, then, happened today? Let us not allow the wonders of this day simply to pass us by. For there was moonlight, and it was just before dawn.
And he was led, with his hands bound, into Pilate’s praetorium.
Those hands that healed the blind and cured the lame!
And the fingers that had created eyelids were fastened with bonds. The one who is a healer by nature was restrained, so that he could not complete his own skillful work.

Is this how you repay the Lord? He was bound—the one who binds the waters in the clouds and by his might releases those in chains. He who grants release to captives was bound, he who freed Lazarus from the bonds of death.
He was led into prison, he who is escorted by angels beyond our knowledge,
he who has heaven as his throne.
And the Creator endured being dragged along by his creation,
the Maker by what he had made, the Creator by what he had created. What, then, came of this? What happened?

“And they,” it says, “did not enter the prison, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.” What great lawlessness! They commit an unjust murder, yet refuse to enter the prison, guarding themselves against defilement when they are already defiled, destroying one sheep by means of another. The Judge of the whole inhabited world waited for judgment. The witness of souls waited for a witness; the Creator was being judged. Human beings sat in judgment, while God stood; and as he stood, he remained silent. The Lord of heaven’s gates stood before human doors. Pilate questioned him, more kindly than the Jews in their malice.

What shall I say? The deeds will indeed reveal the truth. What accusation do you bring against this man? Who can find God guilty? I am compelled to speak Pilate’s words. For Jesus is silent—not because the Word does not know how to speak, but lest by answering he undo the crown of the cross. Did he desire possessions, when he disregarded possessions? Other people’s houses, when he had nowhere to lay his head? Wealth, when he stripped even his own disciples down to their belts? Having no donkey, he took someone else’s donkey to bless your children. State the charge. Show whether you have put him to death justly. The Jews answered him:

“If this man were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” What a great demonstration of his deeds! What a lawless answer! State the evil, and do not [?] your hearers. Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The discerning judge laid the burden upon the heads of the Jews: “You take this accomplice in evil.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” How, then, did you kill Isaiah? How did you kill Zechariah? How did you kill each of the prophets? But “It is not lawful for us to kill” means not that they lack the will, but that they lack the power.

For they had already been deprived of such authority by the Romans. Thus the law is abolished: it now lies in ink, but is inactive in deeds. Jesus abolished it even while bound. But Pilate said, “I find no fault in him.”

Not you alone, Pilate, but neither do the Jews, nor the blind, nor the dead, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor creation, nor all the righteous, the prophets and martyrs. The prophet says, “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” All speak with Pilate, giving him the title “righteous.” Only the Jews oppose him, contending with shouting and wishing to obscure the truth with uproar, and fulfilling Isaiah’s words: “I expected it to produce wine, but it produced thorns; not righteousness, but a desolate outcry.” Such is the vineyard of the Jews,

bearing an outcry as its fruit. While this was happening, Pilate could neither speak nor hear because of the assembled tumult, and civil strife seemed likely to break out. For his wife sent him a message, proving a good helper by restraining her husband as he was being urged on. She said, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man. If you can, release him; if you cannot, save yourself.” She all but spoke David’s words: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with bloodthirsty men.” “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him in a dream.” She was another Joseph, seeing the truth in dreams and bearing witness against the shouting of the Jews. For it was fitting that they should be defeated by a woman. Rahab the prostitute overcame them; the woman with the flow of blood overcame them; the Canaanite woman overcame them; and now once again a woman stands firmly against them. But the Jews answered him, “We have a law,

and according to our law he must die.” What law? In what words is it declared? In those read today, at any rate: “He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like an innocent lamb, silent before those who shear it, so he does not open his mouth. Because of the lawlessness of my people he was led to death.”
I find these words applicable here, and nowhere else: Jesus,

Righteousness being put to death. Pilate entered the praetorium, giving way to the fury of the Jews and attempting to quench an unquenchable flame. He went in and came out, but only kindled the fire further. For he came out bringing Jesus crowned and clothed in purple, already victorious, already dressed in royal guise. What was being done was intended as an insult, but its symbolism accorded with the nature of his kingship. When they saw him whom they had often seen, whom they had never seen, whom they continually see, they blazed up, burning with their own fire. For it would have been better [?] if they had been consumed by fire.
They raised their Sodom-like cry. They raised it and worked themselves into a frenzy: “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!”
“Do you want me to crucify your king?” They said, “We have no king but Caesar.” Renunciation without persecution; godlessness joined to Egyptian wickedness.
“Are these your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt?” Do you have no king but Caesar?
Who, then, led you through the wilderness? Who fed you? Whom does Moses acclaim when he says, “The Lord reigns forever and ever, and beyond”?
Since, then, you have rejected your own king, remain without a king,

dragging the everlasting yoke of slavery. This took place until the sixth hour. Let us also see the remaining part of the day, for all of it is holy. They took him, crowned. With what thorns? With Jewish
rewards. “I expected it to produce wine for me, but it produced thorns.” He was struck in the face.
He received blows, but was put to shame by nothing. Stand with Jesus and see that God with your eyes.
For what did he say? “Lord, who has believed our report? We saw him, and he had no form

or beauty. Rather, his appearance was dishonored, more disfigured than that of the sons of men.” Did the maker of all beauty have no beauty? For he mourned the wickedness of the Jews, being a man afflicted with wounds and knowing how to endure pain.
A man, not God.
For it was as a man, and not as God, that he was wounded.
Who, then, is this man of many pains and many troubles, rejected by everyone? Can it be that he suffers justly?
He bears our sins and accepts pain for us.
“I find no fault in this man.” But he was not ashamed of the reproachful [?]. Though he suffered so much, he remained beyond suffering.
He was wounded and spat upon; he received dishonor, yet he himself remains honored and glorious. Of those who sin [?], as someone—Isaiah—said to them:

“And we thought him to be in pain, wounded and afflicted. But he was wounded because of our sins and suffered pain because of our transgressions.” So was he, then, and were we wounded by him [?]? By his wound we were healed.
A dead man, a physician to the dead; a wounded man, a physician to people suffering many pains.
An herb to counter the wound. But how long will you flatter our indifference, O man?
State more clearly what we are seeking: “He was led like a lamb to slaughter.”

And like a lamb, a good sheep handed over to wicked cooks, he is slaughtered. O Jews, do not shear the sheep! But if you shear it, spare the sheep that bears good fruit. Others were also led with him, two criminals. For our discourse comes to the tenth hour of the day. Let no one condemn his own life. I had intended to pass over this account, since I have often told it to you. But I see the robber continually pressing me. And no wonder: he forced even the gates of paradise, cleverly turning the Savior away from us. On the cross stood a lamb and two wolves. But one remained earthly in his disposition, while the other was already being transformed, saying, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” O the power of Jesus! The robber is already a prophet, preaching from the cross.

“Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” What royal thing do you see, O robber? The blows, the spitting, the nails, or the wood, and the insults of the Jews, and the spear already being drawn by the soldiers? “But I see,” he said, “angels standing around him. I see the sun fleeing, the curtain being torn, the earth trembling, and the dead already preparing to run.” Jesus, who accepts everyone, who also, to those who came at the eleventh

hour, gave the same denarius. “Truly, truly, I say to you.” Receive this “truly” yourself, O robber: you who today are a robber, today are a son. “Today you will be with me in paradise. I, who drove you out, am bringing you in—I who closed the gates of paradise, who fenced it off with a flaming spear. For unless I bring you in, the gates will remain closed. Come, O robber, who have defeated the devil and been crowned over him, who have seen a man and worshiped God, who have thrown down your former weapon

and taken up a trustworthy one.” With things being so, and everything illuminated—the sun from the sky, the wood from the gardens, the gall from the Jews, the seamless robe from the woven fabrics, the purple for clothing from the sea, and the iron from the mines, the spear and the nails—and with the twin streams of blood and water poured out, the Savior was doing his work. “Father, forgive them their sin.” Whom was he to forgive? The Greeks or the Jews? Strangers or foreigners? Everyone without distinction. For he spoke once, and the deed is continually being done. [?] Was it only of the soldiers that he said, “Forgive”? He speaks throughout all ages, and he speaks continually, and whoever wishes receives. They all gathered in Pilate’s praetorium. What did they say? “We know that this deceiver said, while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’”
Do you know very well? Do you remember very well that he will rise? He secures the tomb. For you are securing it for me. Keep watch.

the dead man, so that he does not escape. “Do you have a guard?” he said. “Go and secure it as you know how. You killed him as you saw fit; make your arrangements as you know how. Keep watch. If you had not guarded him, you would have left grounds for an accusation against me. But now I hand him over to you yourselves. When he was alive, he was held by you; but when he was killed, he was hidden from you all.” Let us therefore remain watchful, not sleeping, so that we may see the deep sleep of the Jews and celebrate with the heavenly hosts in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
